title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in Lisbon: Route Planning at Scale ⚡
description: Watch Bidirectional Dijkstra slice the search space by expanding from both start and goal until paths meet. This city-grid visualization shows why modern route planning engines scale faster on large maps.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra: How Modern Route Planners Scale — inside high-scale navigation engines, Bidirectional Dijkstra visualised ⚡

In this Lisbon (Alfama) map grid, we run two Dijkstra frontiers at once:
1) Forward search expands from the start.
2) Backward search expands from the goal.
3) When the frontiers meet, we stitch the best route (min total cost).

Why it feels faster: fewer explored nodes than classic single-source Dijkstra, especially when start↔goal are far apart. It’s still guaranteed optimal on weighted graphs—just with a smarter “meet-in-the-middle” strategy.

Takeaway: fewer expansions → quicker time-to-first-route, which matters for shortest path at scale in route planning engines.

Debate question: Would you rather trade extra bookkeeping for fewer node visits, or keep it simple with classic Dijkstra?
